title: Error Handling Concepts
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and core rule of error handling concepts using at least one example.
Trace or adapt a minimal C++ example related to error handling concepts and state its expected result.
Identify one precondition, error case, lifetime issue, portability assumption or version constraint relevant to the topic.

content.intro: Error Handling Concepts focuses on the decisions and observable behavior named by the subtopics below. The aim is to explain the rule, predict what a small program should do, and then confirm the result with a focused check.
content.why_it_matters: Error Handling Concepts matters because try missing files, malformed input and empty data, and verify both the result and the failure path. Connect this lesson to the earlier module prerequisites and use it as a building block rather than an isolated term.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
I/O can fail because of stream state, filesystem conditions or malformed data. Robust programs check operations and report errors without leaving state half-updated.

Error Handling Concepts focuses on the decisions and observable behavior named by the subtopics below. The aim is to explain the rule, predict what a small program should do, and then confirm the result with a focused check.

Try missing files, malformed input and empty data, and verify both the result and the failure path.

content_blocks.title: Minimal example: Error Handling Concepts
content_blocks.run_instructions: Save as `example.cpp`. Compile using `g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic example.cpp -o example; then run ./example (Windows: .\example.exe).` The CodeLeaf page shows reference output only; it does not execute C++ learner code.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the example, rebuild with the same standard and warning flags, and rerun the same input. If the example is nondeterministic or depends on platform support, record that constraint instead of expecting byte-for-byte identical output.
content_blocks.limitations: The built-in CodeLeaf page does not execute C++ in a sandbox. Compile local teaching examples only; arbitrary learner code requires a separately deployed isolated runner with CPU, memory, process, filesystem and network limits.
content_blocks.explanation: Error handling begins by stating valid input and choosing how failure is reported; callers must check the failure path.

items.title: Choosing an Error-Handling Strategy
items.text: Compare the alternatives in Choosing an Error-Handling Strategy by their semantics, constraints and trade-offs; use the simpler option that satisfies the real requirement.

content_blocks.title: Guided practice
content_blocks.text: Before changing the example, predict the output and name the rule that produces it. Then modify one line to demonstrate syntax, compile-time and run-time errors, and add a test for one boundary or failure scenario. Keep the experiment small enough that another learner can reproduce it.

content_blocks.title: Version, safety and portability note
content_blocks.text: Use standard C++ rather than compiler-specific behavior unless the lesson explicitly labels the dependency. Feature support varies by compiler version and standard-library implementation. Check the references and prefer explicit diagnostics to assumptions.

content.task: Extend the example for Error Handling Concepts with one additional valid case and one boundary or failure case. State your expected result first, then compile with the documented C++20 warning flags.
task_acceptance_criteria: The code compiles in the documented standard mode with warnings enabled.
The predicted output matches the actual result for the added case.
One relevant boundary, lifetime, portability or error case is tested or documented.
hints: Start by isolating the central rule from Error Handling Concepts.
Trace values or object lifetimes before changing the program.
Use a small boundary test and check the compiler diagnostic rather than assuming the behavior.
summary: Error Handling Concepts is about a concrete language rule or engineering decision, not only terminology.
Keep the important preconditions and trade-offs visible when applying error handling concepts.
Use explicit build settings and focused tests to support the claim that the example behaves as expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming one successful example proves every case.
common_mistakes.why: It may miss an invalid input, boundary, error path or implementation difference.
common_mistakes.fix: Write down the preconditions and test at least one ordinary case plus an edge or failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a language feature without checking its requirements.
common_mistakes.why: The code may depend on a standard version, an object lifetime or an API precondition.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the explicit standard mode and verify the relevant rule and compiler/library support.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring compiler diagnostics or simplifying away ownership and error behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Warnings and explicit contracts often expose a defect before it becomes a runtime problem.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile with warnings, keep the smallest reproducible sample and state what happens when an operation fails.
